parts.markdown:
Use our free **Colorado paycheck calculator** to estimate your take-home pay after federal income tax, Colorado income tax, Social Security, Medicare, paid family leave contributions and applicable local occupational taxes.

Enter your annual salary or hourly wage, choose your pay frequency and customize your withholding information to understand how much money you could receive on payday.

Whether you work in Denver, Colorado Springs, Boulder, Fort Collins or another Colorado community, understanding your estimated net income can help you compare job offers, manage housing expenses and establish realistic financial goals.

## How to Use the Colorado Paycheck Calculator

If your pay stub lists Colorado paid family leave contributions, include the amount under other deductions. Enter each deduction once.

Start by choosing whether you receive an annual salary or hourly wages.

Enter your earnings before taxes and select your payment frequency. Enter federal and Colorado income tax withheld for the pay period from your pay stub.

Include retirement contributions, healthcare premiums and other employee deductions.

If occupational privilege tax was withheld, enter the amount from that pay period.

Review your results to see your estimated gross income, federal taxes, Colorado withholding, payroll contributions and take-home pay.

For more accurate calculations, use your most recent payroll statement and withholding certificates.

## Colorado Payroll Taxes in 2026

Colorado employees may encounter the following payroll deductions.

Your actual deductions depend on your earnings, employment location, withholding elections and employee benefits.

Colorado's payroll calculation requires particular attention to its paid family leave program and the occupational taxes imposed by certain municipalities.

## How Colorado Income Tax Withholding Works

Colorado uses a flat-rate approach to income taxation. Its 2026 employer withholding worksheet applies a rate of 4.4% to the appropriate annualized taxable wage amount after accounting for the employee's withholding allowance.

Employers calculate withholding using Form DR 1098, the Colorado Withholding Worksheet for Employers.

When an employee has not supplied a custom withholding allowance through Form DR 0004, the standard annual withholding allowances for 2026 are:

parts.caption: How Colorado Income Tax Withholding Works

parts.markdown:
These are payroll withholding allowances, not the standard deductions used to calculate your annual federal income tax return.

The withholding calculation generally involves annualizing taxable wages, subtracting the appropriate allowance, applying the withholding rate and converting the result back to the relevant pay period.

Additional withholding requested by the employee is then included.

Review the official [Colorado withholding worksheet](https://tax.colorado.gov/DR1098) for the complete methodology.

## Colorado State Income Tax Calculation Example

Suppose an employee earns $65,000 annually and receives 26 biweekly paychecks.

The employee is single, has no custom Colorado withholding allowance and receives $2,500 in taxable wages each pay period.

Annualized wages:

$2,500 × 26 = $65,000

Subtract the standard withholding allowance:

$65,000 − $5,500 = $59,500

Calculate the annualized withholding amount:

$59,500 × 4.4% = $2,618

Convert the result into biweekly withholding:

$2,618 ÷ 26 = approximately $100.69

This example assumes ordinary withholding conditions without additional requested deductions or exemptions.

Your final annual Colorado income tax liability may differ from the amount withheld throughout the year.

## Understanding Colorado Form DR 0004

Colorado employees can optionally complete Form DR 0004 to customize state income tax withholding.

The form allows employees to provide an annual withholding allowance and request an additional fixed amount to be withheld each pay period.

If you do not submit the form, your employer generally calculates Colorado withholding using the applicable information from your federal Form W-4.

Employees with multiple jobs, additional income, eligible deductions or expected tax credits may benefit from reviewing their withholding elections.

A lower withholding amount does not necessarily reduce your final income tax liability.

Download the current [Colorado Employee Withholding Certificate](https://tax.colorado.gov/DR0004) to review your options.

## Colorado Family and Medical Leave Insurance

Colorado's Family and Medical Leave Insurance program, commonly called FAMLI, provides qualifying employees with partial wage replacement during eligible periods of leave.

The program can support workers who need time away from employment for qualifying medical conditions, family caregiving and bonding with a new child.

For 2026, the total standard FAMLI premium is 0.88% of covered wages. Employees generally contribute up to half of this amount, equivalent to 0.44%.

Employers may cover part or all of the employee's share.

The program generally uses the annual Social Security wage ceiling, which is $184,500 in 2026.

Assuming the full employee share applies:

parts.markdown:
The maximum standard annual employee contribution at the 0.44% rate is $811.80.

Approved private plans and certain public-sector employment arrangements may result in different deductions or coverage requirements.

Visit the official [Colorado FAMLI program website](https://famli.colorado.gov/) to learn more about contributions and benefits.

## Denver Occupational Privilege Tax

Some Colorado municipalities impose occupational privilege taxes on employees working within their boundaries.

Denver's employee occupational privilege tax is a notable example.

Employees who earn at least $500 in a calendar month from qualifying work performed in Denver are generally subject to an employee tax of $5.75 for that month.

Denver also imposes a separate employer contribution of $4.00. This employer contribution should not be deducted from employee net pay as though it were an employee tax.

The employee deduction is based on qualifying employment activity rather than simply living in Denver.

Because the tax applies monthly, employees receiving weekly or biweekly paychecks should not automatically deduct $5.75 from every paycheck.

Consult the [City and County of Denver occupational tax guidance](https://www.denvergov.org/Government/Agencies-Departments-Offices/Agencies-Departments-Offices-Directory/Department-of-Finance/Our-Divisions/Treasury/Business-Tax-Information/Business-Tax-FAQ) for official requirements.

Other Colorado municipalities may have different occupational tax arrangements.

## Federal Payroll Taxes for Colorado Employees

Employees in Colorado generally pay federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare alongside applicable state deductions.

Federal income tax withholding depends on earnings, filing status, payroll frequency and Form W-4 information.

Social Security applies at 6.2% of covered wages, subject to the 2026 annual wage limit of $184,500.

Ordinary Medicare applies at 1.45% of covered wages without a standard annual wage ceiling.

Employers generally withhold an additional 0.9% when Medicare-covered wages paid by that employer exceed $200,000 during the calendar year.

Read the [IRS Employer's Tax Guide](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15) for additional information about federal payroll contributions.

## Colorado Paycheck Example: $65,000 Salary

Consider an employee earning $65,000 annually and receiving $2,500 biweekly.

Assume the employee is single, has the standard Colorado withholding allowance, has not reached any annual contribution limits and pays the full standard employee FAMLI contribution.

Approximately $2,197.06 remains before federal income tax withholding, applicable occupational taxes and other employee deductions.

If a Denver occupational privilege tax deduction is due during that paycheck, an additional $5.75 may be withheld.

Use the calculator with your actual federal withholding information to estimate your complete take-home paycheck.

## Colorado Hourly Paycheck Calculator

Hourly employees can calculate gross pay by multiplying their hourly wage by regular hours and adding qualifying overtime compensation.

Consider an employee earning $30 per hour who works 40 regular hours and six overtime hours at time-and-a-half.

Regular pay:

$30 × 40 = $1,200

Overtime pay:

$30 × 1.5 × 6 = $270

Total gross pay:

$1,470

Colorado has state overtime requirements that may apply in addition to federal weekly overtime rules. Certain covered employees can qualify for overtime based on daily or consecutive hours worked.

Consult the [Colorado Department of Labor and Employment](https://cdle.colorado.gov/dlss) for current wage and overtime requirements.

## Comparing Colorado Salaries and Living Expenses

When evaluating employment opportunities in Colorado, compare estimated net earnings alongside living expenses.

Housing and commuting costs can vary significantly between metropolitan Denver, mountain communities and smaller cities.

Employer retirement contributions, healthcare coverage, transportation benefits and remote working arrangements can also influence the overall value of a job offer.

Use our [salary-to-hourly calculator](/calculators/salary-to-hourly-calculator/) to compare compensation arrangements and our [emergency fund calculator](/savings/emergency-fund-calculator/) to establish a financial cushion based on your expected monthly expenses.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is Colorado's paycheck withholding rate in 2026?

Colorado's official 2026 employer withholding worksheet uses a rate of 4.4% after applicable withholding allowances. Your actual deduction depends on taxable wages, filing information and any custom withholding elections.

### What is the Colorado FAMLI deduction on my paycheck?

FAMLI is Colorado's paid family and medical leave insurance program. The standard employee contribution is generally up to 0.44% of covered wages in 2026, subject to the applicable annual wage ceiling.

### Do employees working in Denver pay an additional local tax?

Qualifying employees earning at least $500 in a calendar month from work performed in Denver generally owe an employee occupational privilege tax of $5.75 for that month.
